column1: What tradeoff do transaction isolation levels control?
column2:
Data consistency versus concurrency.
Stronger isolation can require more locking or version management.
Review source

column1: Which isolation level allows reading another transaction's uncommitted changes?
column2:
READ UNCOMMITTED.
A dirty read can reflect a change that the other transaction later rolls back.
Review source

column1: Why can repeated READ COMMITTED queries see different committed values for the same row within one transaction?
column2:
Other transactions can commit changes between statements.
Preventing dirty reads does not prevent nonrepeatable reads.
Review source

column1: With RCSI disabled, how does READ COMMITTED protect ordinary SELECT reads?
column2:
Shared data locks.
These read locks are released during or at the end of the statement, rather than held until commit.
Review source

column1: How does REPEATABLE READ protect rows already read by a transaction?
column2:
It holds shared locks on the read data until the transaction ends.
Other transactions can still insert matching rows, so phantom reads remain possible.
Review source

column1: How does SERIALIZABLE protect an indexed search range against phantom inserts?
column2:
Key-range locks held until the transaction ends.
These locks prevent other transactions from inserting keys into the protected range.
Review source

column1: Which database option makes READ COMMITTED use row-versioned reads?
column2:
READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT.
Read committed snapshot isolation (RCSI) changes READ COMMITTED behavior rather than adding a sixth session isolation level.
Review source

column1: What committed data does each ordinary SELECT see under RCSI?
column2:
Data as it existed at the start of that statement.
Later statements in the same transaction can see other transactions' later commits.
Review source

column1: Which isolation level provides one consistent versioned view across multiple queries in a transaction?
column2:
SNAPSHOT.
The snapshot is established at first data access, and reads also see the transaction's own writes.
Review source

column1: What blocking can still occur between transactions modifying the same row under RCSI?
column2:
Writer/writer blocking.
Versioned reads do not allow conflicting writes to proceed simultaneously.
Review source

column1: What happens when SNAPSHOT updates a row changed and committed by another transaction after its snapshot began?
column2:
An update conflict aborts the transaction.
Handle the failure and retry the entire transaction, not just its UPDATE.
Review source

column1: Why can READ COMMITTED still oversell stock with a separate SELECT followed by an unconditional decrement?
column2:
Both transactions can read the same committed stock before either updates it.
Check availability in the UPDATE predicate instead of trusting an earlier SELECT.
Review source

column1: Which T-SQL value confirms whether a conditional UPDATE affected the single product row?
column2:
@@ROWCOUNT, checked immediately after the UPDATE.
Create the order only when the count is 1, within the same transaction.
Review source

column1: What does lock after qualification (LAQ) do before locking a row for modification?
column2:
It tests the predicate using the latest row version committed as of statement start.
Rows that do not qualify can be skipped without waiting on the writer.
Review source

column1: With optimized locking enabled, which isolation configuration does LAQ require?
column2:
READ COMMITTED with READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT enabled.
LAQ is not used under stricter isolation levels or conflicting locking hints.
Review source

column1: Under LAQ, what happens if a qualifying row changes before the engine can update it?
column2:
The engine rechecks the predicate after resolving the write conflict.
It updates the row only if the row still qualifies.
Review source

column1: Why avoid waiting for user input or external API calls inside an open database transaction?
column2:
Long waits can prolong lock or row-version retention.
This can increase blocking or the space needed for retained versions.
Review source

column1: Which lock can block even a READ UNCOMMITTED SELECT during a schema change?
column2:
A schema-modification (Sch-M) lock.
The SELECT still acquires a schema-stability (Sch-S) lock, which conflicts with Sch-M.
Review source

column1: Which concurrency model uses row versions instead of shared data locks for ordinary reads?
column2:
Optimistic concurrency.
Write operations still use locks to protect their changes.
Review source

column1: Which SQL Server table hint requests update locks for reads and holds them until the transaction ends?
column2:
UPDLOCK.
If the operation takes a table-level lock, it uses an exclusive lock instead.
Review source

column1: Which isolation level does the SQL Server HOLDLOCK table hint apply?
column2:
SERIALIZABLE.
It applies to the referenced table or view for the transaction's duration.
Review source

column1: Which table hint requests locking reads instead of row versions under READ COMMITTED with READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT enabled?
column2:
READCOMMITTEDLOCK.
It requests shared data locks for the referenced table.
Review source

column1: What is the default READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT setting in Azure SQL Managed Instance?
column2:
OFF.
Ordinary READ COMMITTED reads therefore use shared locks unless the database configuration changes.
Review source
